name: grpc-loads-multiple-skills
description: Tests the core orchestration rule: a gRPC task loads the primary skill PLUS its applicable secondary skills together, not a single skill
prompt: I'm about to build a gRPC service in Go. Before I write any code, which of the samber/cc-skills-golang skills should be loaded for this task, and which is primary?
trap: A naive model treats this as a single-skill task (just gRPC) or skips skill routing entirely and starts writing gRPC code, missing that testing and error-handling secondaries must load at the same time

assertions.text: Names golang-grpc as the primary skill
Names golang-testing as a secondary skill to also load
Names golang-error-handling as a secondary skill to also load
States that the primary and secondary skills should be loaded together / at the start, not one at a time
Does NOT jump straight into writing gRPC implementation code instead of identifying skills

name: new-project-layout-routing
description: Tests routing for setting up a new project structure, including its multiple secondary skills
prompt: I'm starting a brand-new Go project from scratch and want to set up the directory/project structure correctly. Which Go skills apply?
trap: A naive model recommends a generic layout (e.g. golang-standards/project-layout) from memory without identifying golang-project-layout as primary or its DI/lint/design-pattern secondaries

assertions.text: Names golang-project-layout as the primary skill
Names golang-design-patterns as a skill to also load
Names golang-dependency-injection as a skill to also load
Names golang-lint as a skill to also load
Loads multiple skills together rather than treating project setup as a single-skill task

name: performance-cluster-disambiguation
description: Tests the performance-cluster boundary: measure first with benchmark, fix with performance, root-cause with troubleshooting
prompt: My Go HTTP handler is slow in production and I'm not sure why. I want to make it faster. Which Go skill owns this, and what's the right order to bring skills in?
trap: A naive model immediately suggests optimizations (sync.Pool, caching, fewer allocations) without measuring, conflating measurement, optimization, and root-cause into one undifferentiated 'performance' answer

assertions.text: Distinguishes measurement (golang-benchmark) from optimization (golang-performance)
Says to measure/profile first (golang-benchmark) before applying optimization patterns
Attributes optimization patterns to golang-performance
For a production slowness symptom, brings in golang-observability (metrics/traces) and/or golang-troubleshooting for root cause
Does NOT recommend specific optimizations as the first step before any measurement

name: safety-vs-security-boundary
description: Tests the correctness-vs-threat boundary: nil-pointer panic is golang-safety (internal bug), not golang-security (external threat)
prompt: My Go service keeps panicking with a nil pointer dereference under certain inputs. Is this a security issue? Which Go skill should I load to address it?
trap: A naive model may label a nil-pointer panic a security vulnerability and route it to security tooling, instead of recognizing it as an internal correctness bug owned by golang-safety

assertions.text: Routes the nil pointer panic to golang-safety as the owning skill
Explains golang-safety covers internal correctness bugs (nil panics, etc.) while golang-security covers external threats (injection, crypto, secrets)
Does NOT classify a nil pointer dereference as a security vulnerability owned by golang-security
May also bring in golang-troubleshooting to debug the existing crash

name: math-rand-token-security
description: Tests routing a predictable-randomness token issue to golang-security (external threat), not golang-safety
prompt: I'm generating session tokens in my Go app using math/rand. Is that fine? Which Go skill covers this?
trap: A naive model may say math/rand is fine or treat it as a correctness/safety concern, missing that predictable randomness is an external-threat issue owned by golang-security (use crypto/rand)

assertions.text: Routes the issue to golang-security
Identifies that math/rand produces predictable output and is unsafe for tokens
Recommends crypto/rand instead of math/rand
Frames this as an external threat (security) rather than an internal correctness bug (safety)

name: di-cluster-lifecycle-routing
description: Tests the DI cluster boundary: lifecycle hooks route to uber-fx, not the lower-level uber-dig
prompt: I'm adding dependency injection to my Go service and I need lifecycle hooks (start/stop) managed by the DI container. Which DI skill should I use?
trap: A naive model picks dig or wire generically, not knowing fx is the lifecycle framework built on top of dig and is the correct choice when lifecycle hooks are required

assertions.text: Recommends golang-uber-fx for lifecycle hooks
Distinguishes uber-fx (lifecycle framework) from uber-dig (lower-level runtime reflection container)
Notes that golang-dependency-injection is where to start for the library-selection decision
Does NOT recommend google-wire for the lifecycle-hooks requirement

name: samber-functional-cluster
description: Tests the samber/* functional cluster boundary: finite slice transform = lo, optional value without nil = mo, event stream = ro
prompt: Two separate questions for my Go code using the samber libraries: (1) I want to transform a slice of users into a map keyed by ID. (2) I want to return an optional value without using nil. Which samber skill/helper for each?
trap: A naive model conflates the three samber libraries or invents helpers, instead of routing finite transforms to lo (lo.KeyBy) and optional-without-nil to mo (mo.Option)

assertions.text: Routes the slice-to-map transform to golang-samber-lo
References lo.KeyBy (or lo.Associate/lo.SliceToMap) for the keyed-map transform
Routes the optional-without-nil case to golang-samber-mo
References mo.Option (mo.Some/mo.None) for the optional value
Does NOT route the optional value to golang-samber-lo or golang-samber-ro

name: package-lookup-vs-management
description: Tests the package-discovery cluster: looking up versions/CVEs of an existing path is golang-pkg-go-dev, not dependency-management or general web search
prompt: I want to know what versions of github.com/samber/lo exist and whether any of them have known CVEs. How should I find this out in the samber Go skill ecosystem?
trap: A naive model suggests a generic web search or running go list / go get, missing that golang-pkg-go-dev is the dedicated read-only lookup layer for versions, docs, importers, and CVEs of an existing path

assertions.text: Routes the lookup to golang-pkg-go-dev
Identifies pkg-go-dev as the read-only fact-lookup layer for an existing import path (versions, docs, importers, CVEs)
Distinguishes pkg-go-dev (look up facts) from golang-dependency-management (edit go.mod / upgrade) and golang-security (whole-tree govulncheck scan)
Does NOT recommend Context7 or a generic web search as the primary way to look up the Go package facts

name: cli-from-scratch-three-skills
description: Tests that building a CLI from scratch loads the architecture, command-tree, and config-layering skills together
prompt: I'm building a new Go CLI from scratch. It will have a tree of subcommands and needs to read config from flags, env vars, and a config file. Which Go skills should I load?
trap: A naive model just suggests cobra and starts writing commands, missing the CLI-architecture skill (exit codes, signals, stdio) and the viper config-layering skill, and not loading the cluster together

assertions.text: Names golang-cli for CLI architecture (exit codes, signal handling, stdio)
Names golang-spf13-cobra for the command tree / subcommands
Names golang-spf13-viper for layering config from flags, env, and file
Loads all three skills together rather than only suggesting cobra

name: configure-mode-required-block
description: Tests Configure mode mechanics: add a '## Required Go skills' block with fully-qualified identifiers to the project agent config file
prompt: On my team we want golang-security and golang-testing to ALWAYS load for our Go repo, not just when someone mentions them. How do I force-trigger these skills for the whole project?
trap: A naive model suggests adding a vague note to a README or relying on prompt phrasing, instead of using Configure mode to add a structured '## Required Go skills' block to CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md with fully-qualified skill IDs

assertions.text: Adds a section titled '## Required Go skills' to the project's agent config file
Targets CLAUDE.md and/or AGENTS.md (the project agent config) as the file to edit
Uses fully-qualified identifiers like samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-security and samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-testing
States the block makes the listed skills always load regardless of whether the user mentions them
Checks for / preserves idempotency (does not duplicate an existing block) or mentions the startup token cost of always-loaded skills

name: structs-interfaces-vs-design-patterns
description: Tests the type-vs-architecture gap: pointer-vs-value receiver is golang-structs-interfaces; functional options / middleware is golang-design-patterns
prompt: Two design questions for my Go API: (1) Should this method use a value or pointer receiver? (2) How do I implement the functional options pattern for my constructor? Which skill owns each?
trap: A naive model treats both as one 'design' topic and answers from memory, instead of splitting low-level type mechanics (structs-interfaces) from architectural patterns (design-patterns)

assertions.text: Routes the value-vs-pointer receiver question to golang-structs-interfaces
Routes the functional options pattern to golang-design-patterns
Explains the boundary: structs-interfaces owns low-level type mechanics; design-patterns owns architectural patterns
May also reference golang-naming for the constructor name

name: cancel-goroutine-load-both
description: Tests the goroutine-vs-cancel overlap: cancelling goroutines via context loads BOTH golang-concurrency and golang-context
prompt: I have a worker goroutine and I want to cancel it from the outside when a request is aborted. Which Go skill covers this — concurrency or context?
trap: A naive model picks only one of the two skills, missing that this overlap case requires loading both (context owns the cancel API, concurrency owns the goroutine select-on-Done coordination)

assertions.text: Says to load BOTH golang-concurrency and golang-context, not just one
Attributes the context cancellation API (context.WithCancel / ctx.Done) to golang-context
Attributes the goroutine coordination (select on ctx.Done() in the worker) to golang-concurrency
Does NOT claim a single skill exclusively owns the entire cancel-a-goroutine task
